examples.problem_statement: The (i) _________ child approached the diving board; (ii) _________ water in the first place, he found the prospect of jumping into it from some height even more frightening. Blank (i): tremulous / coltish / cumbersome. Blank (ii): beguiled by / chary of / repulsed by.

solution.operation: Collect the sentence's clue words about the child's state: "frightening", "even more frightening"
solution.result: Every clue in the sentence points to fear
solution.description: Gather the descriptive clues the sentence gives about the child before touching either blank, so both blanks are filled from the same established direction: fear.

solution.operation: Match blank (i) against the fear direction: tremulous vs. coltish vs. cumbersome
solution.description: Choose the blank (i) word that expresses fear; tremulous matches the fear clues best, while coltish and cumbersome describe something other than being scared.

solution.operation: Gauge the intensity blank (ii) needs: diving is "even more frightening" than the water itself, so the water feeling must be a milder fear
solution.result: Blank (ii) = chary of, meaning suspicious or slightly scared of
solution.description: Set the strength of blank (ii) from the comparison: because jumping is described as more frightening than the water, the child's feeling toward water must be a less extreme version of frightened, which is chary of.

key_reminders: Fill both blanks from the same clue direction the sentence establishes.
A comparative like "even more frightening" fixes the relative intensity of the two blanks: the earlier feeling must be the milder one.
common_mistakes: Taking "repulsed by" for blank (ii): it is a fear/aversion word but too extreme to be outranked by "even more frightening".
Reading "beguiled by" as fitting the fear direction when it points the opposite way, toward attraction.

examples.problem_statement: In the figure above, points A, B, C, and D lie in that order on a circle whose diameter is 10, and ABCD is the quadrilateral they form. Quantity A: the area of quadrilateral ABCD. Quantity B: 40. Choose: (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.operation: List what is actually given: circle diameter = 10, and A, B, C, D lie on the circle in the order shown
solution.result: Only the diameter and the cyclic order of the four points are fixed
solution.description: Separate the given information from what the picture merely looks like, so you know exactly which facts you are allowed to use.

solution.operation: Apply the rule that figures are not necessarily drawn to scale, and redraw the circle with A, B, C, D still in the same order but spaced differently
solution.result: The positions of the four points may vary freely as long as their order is preserved
solution.description: Because the figure is not to scale, deliberately vary the point positions to see how much the area of ABCD can move while the given information stays true.

solution.operation: Place A and C opposite each other with B and D very close to C
solution.result: Quadrilateral ABCD collapses and its area is very close to 0, so the area can be less than 40
solution.description: Test the first extreme arrangement by crowding three vertices together, which squeezes the quadrilateral flat and drives its area below Quantity B.

solution.operation: Place A, B, C, D evenly spaced around the circle and draw the diameters AC and BD
solution.result: AC and BD are perpendicular bisectors of each other, cutting ABCD into four right triangles
solution.description: Test the opposite extreme by spreading the points evenly, then add the two diagonals, which for evenly spaced points are perpendicular diameters that split the quadrilateral into four congruent right triangles.

solution.operation: Each right triangle has legs equal to the radius: \frac{1}{2}(5)(5)
solution.description: Find the area of one of the four right triangles, whose two legs are each half of the diameter 10, that is, the radius 5.
Total the four congruent triangles to get the area of the evenly spaced quadrilateral, which exceeds Quantity B's 40.

solution.operation: Compare the two cases against Quantity B: one area is near 0 (less than 40), the other is 50 (greater than 40)
solution.result: No single relationship holds for every allowed figure
solution.description: Conclude from the two valid arrangements straddling 40 that Quantity A can be either smaller or larger, so the comparison cannot be settled.

examples.answer: Choice D: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

key_reminders: GRE figures are not necessarily drawn to scale; only the stated facts and the drawn order of points may be assumed.
In a quantitative comparison, one arrangement below the benchmark and one above it forces Choice D.
Diagonals joining diametrically opposite points are diameters, and for evenly spaced points they are perpendicular bisectors of each other.
common_mistakes: Trusting the drawn shape and computing a single area for ABCD instead of varying the point positions.
Stopping after finding the near-zero case and answering Choice B, without checking the evenly spaced case that gives 50.

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. It would have been disingenuous of the candidate to appear ______ when her opponent won the election, but she congratulated the victor nonetheless. (A) gracious (B) ecstatic (C) crestfallen (D) indifferent (E) euphoric (F) disgruntled

solution.operation: Interpret the key word: what reaction by a losing candidate would appear "disingenuous"?
solution.result: A show of delight at her own defeat would be insincere
solution.description: Decide what the blank must mean by reasoning from "disingenuous": the reaction has to be one that would be plainly insincere coming from the loser.

solution.operation: Test the choices against that requirement: ecstatic, euphoric
solution.result: Both would be highly disingenuous, and they are alike in meaning
solution.description: Pick out the choices that satisfy the insincerity requirement and also match each other, since the completed sentences must be alike in meaning.

solution.operation: Check the remaining tempting choice, gracious
solution.result: It fits the blank, but no other offered word is nearly alike in meaning to it, so it is rejected
solution.description: Rule out gracious by the pairing requirement: a word that fits the sentence but has no near-synonym among the choices cannot be part of the answer.

examples.answer: Choice B: ecstatic AND Choice E: euphoric

key_reminders: Sentence equivalence requires two choices that both fit the sentence and are alike in meaning to each other.
A choice that fits the blank but has no near-synonym among the options is automatically out.
common_mistakes: Selecting gracious because it reads naturally in the sentence, even though it is left without a matching partner.
Pairing crestfallen with disgruntled: those describe a sincere reaction to losing, which would not be disingenuous.
